function.name: give_up
function.arguments: {"reason": "Measured gripper opening is 0.0162, i.e. fully closed on empty air, so the block is still resting on the table at (-0.030,-0.075) and is not held. The trial is at step 783 of 900 and this is call 19 of 20: a close-only move already consumed 79 steps, so the remaining ~117 steps cannot cover a lift, a translation to the bowl and a release. I am stopping rather than spending the last call on a motion that cannot finish the placement.", "hindsight": "Concrete facts for a future agent on this rig. (1) Motion is heavily truncated: the tool budget for one call is shared with the gripper, and a gripper latch costs ~80 control steps, so any move_to that includes gripper=0/1 leaves only a few steps for the arm and barely moves it; never bundle a long translation with a close/open, and never rely on a commanded target being reached. (2) Pure lateral moves of 10-20 cm advanced only 2-6 steps (~1-4 cm) in my run, so most of my 20 calls were spent on localisation rather than travel; plan at most ~8 localisation calls. (3) The block was at world (x=-0.030, y=-0.075) on the table (table top z=0.80, block ~3 cm), the blue bowl was at roughly (0.0,+0.02), i.e. only ~10 cm from the block; my early axis-calibration moves drifted to x=+0.04,y=+0.07 and wasted ~10 calls. (4) Fingertip pads sit about 2.5-3 cm below the reported eef_pos, so to straddle a 3 cm block the eef z target should be ~0.855-0.865; at eef z=0.876 the pads were still above the block top and closed on air. (5) Gripper measurement is effectively binary here: 0.98 = open, 0.016 = closed on air; a real grasp should read intermediate, so re-check that number after every close instead of trusting the images. (6) Camera axes: in the side view image-horizontal is world x (bowl/−x at left, arm base at right) and it is a good metric ruler (~0.5 mm/px at this depth); in the front view image-horizontal is also x but depth (y) is hard to read; the wrist view rotates with yaw, so do not assume image right = any fixed world axis — verify with one small single-axis move before trusting it. (7) The wrist camera looking straight down shows the finger gap and the block between the pads, which is the most reliable lateral alignment cue once the hand is low."}
